title: Hybrid Ferromagnet-SNSPDs: Single photon induced order-to-disorder transition in ferromagnets coupled to thin film superconductors
authors: Leif Bauer, Daien He, Sathwik Bharadwaj, Zubin Jacob
abstract: The development of midwave and longwave infrared single photon detectors is crucial for their emerging applications in spectroscopy, remote sensing, exoplanet detection, and free space quantum communications. However, existing sensors need to be operated at extremely low temperatures (0.08-0.9K) to reduce dark noise and hence require the use of advanced cryogenics such as dilution refrigerators or $^3$He cryogens, significantly limiting applications. Here we propose a vortex-engineering approach based on a hybrid phase transition in a ferromagnet/superconductor bilayer to increase the operating temperature of infrared single photon detectors up to 3.75K. We show that the introduction of a ferromagnetic layer produces a local magnetic field which impedes vortex crossing in the superconductor, reducing dark noise. When a single photon is incident, the photon-induced hotspot causes an order-to-disorder transition in the ferromagnet, leading to a vortex-induced phase transition in the superconducting layer. By engineering the ferromagnet's Curie temperature to be close to the device's operating temperature, single photon sensitivity can be achieved at increased operating temperatures. We predict at midwave/longwave infrared wavelengths (3-14$μ$m) the operating temperature can be raised to 3.25-3.75K, enabling significantly simpler cooling systems.
summary: The paper proposes using a hybrid Ferromagnet/Superconductor structure to create highly sensitive single-photon detectors that operate at significantly higher temperatures than previously possible. By engineering the magnetic coupling such that an incident photon triggers a controlled phase transition in the ferromagnet, the superconducting detection mechanism is activated efficiently while minimizing dark noise. This breakthrough promises simpler and more practical quantum sensing applications.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop infrared single-photon detectors that operate at significantly higher temperatures than current cryogenic limits (T < 1K) by engineering the operating mechanism.
main_result: A hybrid Ferromagnet/Superconductor bilayer can achieve high sensitivity up to 3.25–3.75K by coupling a photon-induced order-to-disorder transition in the ferromagnet to a superconducting phase transition.
method: The analysis uses vortex-crossing theory, time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau simulations, and atomistic spin dynamics to model the coupled magnetic and superconducting transitions.
model_or_system: The system is a hybrid Ferromagnet/Superconductor (FM/S) bilayer. The mechanism relies on the local heating from an incident photon causing disordering in the FM layer, which modifies the magnetic field profile and lowers the vortex crossing barrier in the superconductor.
key_observables: Noise Equivalent Power (NEP), Dark Count Rate (DCR), System Detection Efficiency (SDE), and operating temperature ($T_{op}$).
important_parameters: Operating Temperature (3.25–3.75K), Curie Temperature ($T_{	ext{Curie}}$) of the FM layer, magnetic field strength ($\sim 40	ext{mT}$), and thermal time constant ($	au$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes that the single-photon event triggers a localized hotspot leading to an order-to-disorder transition in the ferromagnet, which then drives the superconducting detection mechanism.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the operational cycle (no photon vs. photon incidence), show the dependence of DCR and NEP on applied magnetic fields and thermal time constants, and map out potential device designs based on critical temperatures ($T_{	ext{crit}}$, $T_{	ext{Curie}}$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the limitations of current detectors, then proposing the hybrid FM/S structure. It details the underlying physics using vortex-crossing theory and simulations to show how magnetic field engineering allows for higher temperature operation while maintaining high sensitivity.
why_interesting: This work models a non-equilibrium phase transition driven by external stimuli (photons) in a coupled magnet-superconductor system, which has strong parallels with studying energy dissipation and thermalization dynamics in quantum materials.
